detail: supported
It is used for efficient storage and retrieval of volumetric data at multiple resolutions, facilitating interactive rendering of large datasets [S1, S2].

The evidence in both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly describes a method for constructing a multiresolution wavelet tree for volume data. This process involves subdividing data into blocks, applying wavelet transforms, and compressing coefficients (using thresholding, run-length encoding, and Huffman coding), which directly supports the claim of 'efficient storage and retrieval of volumetric data at multiple resolutions'. Furthermore, Source [S1] mentions 'parallel rendering of selected data blocks at various levels of detail' and 'parallel volume rendering', which supports the claim of 'facilitating interactive rendering of large datasets'.
supported

*   **Performance:** The method exhibits good compression ratios when many consecutive zero subsequences are present in the wavelet coefficient sequence, and it is very fast to decompress due to the bit-level run-length encoding scheme [S1, S2].

The claim states that the method exhibits good compression ratios when many consecutive zero subsequences are present and is very fast to decompress due to the bit-level run-length encoding scheme. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'This bit-level run-length encoding scheme exhibits good compression ratio if many consecutive zero subsequences are present in the wavelet coefficient sequence and is very fast to decompress.' Source [S2] contains the exact same sentence. Therefore, every fact in the claim is directly supported by the evidence.
supported

Group the low-pass filtered subblock and the wavelet coefficients [S1, S2].

4.  **Error metric:** A scalar value representing the Mean Square Error (MSE) between the low-resolution data block $B$ and the corresponding raw data in subvolume $V$ [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the section '4 Wavelet Tree Construction with Hierarchical Error Metric Calculation' that 'Our error metric is based on the mean square error (MSE) calculation.' It further defines the variables: 'the data block of n voxels associated with S that approximates the original subvolume V is B.' Although the text cuts off at 'corresponding raw data in sub...', the context clearly links the low-resolution data block B (derived from the wavelet tree structure described in the notes) to the original subvolume V, and defines the error metric as the MSE between them. The notes confirm that B is the 'lower resolution data block' and V is the 'original three-dimensional data' (subvolume). Thus, the claim that the error metric is the MSE between B and the raw data in V is supported by the text.
supported
If the data block is uniform, skip the 3D wavelet transform computation, set the low-pass filtered subblock to that uniform value, and set all corresponding wavelet coefficients to zero [S1, S2].

Both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly state that if a data block is uniform, the 3D wavelet transform computation can be skipped to save space and time. They further specify that in this case, the low-pass filtered subblock should be set to that uniform value and all corresponding wavelet coefficients should be set to zero. This matches the claim exactly.
